reasoning: Extensive scientific research and double-blind, placebo-controlled studies have failed to establish a causal link between monosodium glutamate (MSG) and the cluster of symptoms historically dubbed "Chinese restaurant syndrome" (such as headaches, numbness, and flushing). The concept originated from an anecdotal letter published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1968 rather than rigorous clinical trials. Major food safety and health organizations, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the World Health Organization (WHO), classify MSG as "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS), noting that the human body metabolizes added glutamate identically to naturally occurring glutamate found in foods like tomatoes and parmesan cheese. While a tiny subset of individuals may have mild, transient sensitivity to unusually large doses consumed without food, there is no consistent evidence that typical dietary MSG consumption causes these symptoms.
